title: Damascus and Ephraim Fall Together
summary: The oracle against Damascus announces that the Aramean capital will become a heap of ruins and that Israel, its ally, will share its fate, with only a few gleanings left like olives on a beaten tree. On that day people will turn from the altars and Asherah poles they made to their Maker, because they had forgotten the God of their salvation. The chapter ends with the nations roaring like the sea against God's people, only to be scattered like chaff overnight.
story: The oracles against the nations now turn north. Damascus, capital of Aram (roughly modern Syria), had joined with the northern kingdom of Israel to pressure Judah in the crisis of Isaiah 7 and 8. In those chapters Isaiah told King Ahaz not to fear these two smoldering stubs of firewood, because both would soon be stripped by Assyria. Chapter 17 makes the same point in the form of an oracle, and pointedly puts Israel (called Ephraim and Jacob) inside an oracle addressed to a foreign nation. The people of God who allied with a pagan power will fall with it. Verses 12 to 14 look beyond this particular crisis to the pattern of the nations raging against Zion and being driven away, a theme that will return when Assyria besieges Jerusalem in chapters 36 and 37.
historical:
In the 730s BC Rezin, king of Aram-Damascus, and Pekah, king of Israel, formed an alliance to resist the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III. When Ahaz of Judah refused to join, they marched on Jerusalem to replace him (2 Kings 16:5; Isaiah 7:1-6), a conflict scholars call the Syro-Ephraimite war, around 734 BC. Ahaz appealed to Assyria instead. Tiglath-pileser III took Damascus in 732 BC, killed Rezin, and deported its people (2 Kings 16:9), turning Aram into Assyrian provinces. He also stripped Israel of Galilee and the land east of the Jordan (2 Kings 15:29), and ten years later Samaria itself fell, in 722 BC. The oracle likely dates from shortly before 732 BC.

The cities of Aroer in verse 2 are puzzling, since the best-known Aroer lay on the Arnon in Moab's territory, far south of Damascus; some scholars think the name refers to towns of the region under Aram's control, others follow a different reading found in the Greek translation. Damascus did not remain a ruin. It was rebuilt and has been inhabited ever since, becoming a leading city again under later empires. Readers differ over how that bears on verse 1, a question taken up below.
cultural:
The harvest images of verses 5 and 6 come straight from Israel's fields. Reapers cut grain with a sickle, gathering the stalks in one arm, and the law required that the edges and the fallen ears be left for gleaners, the poor who followed behind (Leviticus 19:9-10). Olives were harvested by beating the branches with poles so the fruit fell, leaving a few berries at the very top that no one could reach. Both pictures describe what is left after the harvesters are done: a handful. The Valley of Rephaim was a fertile plain just southwest of Jerusalem that Isaiah's hearers could see.

Verse 8 names the objects of popular religion. Asherah was a Canaanite goddess, and the Asherahs were wooden poles or stylized trees set up beside altars in her honor; the incense altars were small stands for burning incense, several of which archaeologists have found in Israelite and Canaanite sites. Verses 10 and 11 describe carefully tended plots planted with foreign cuttings that sprout quickly and wither. Some scholars connect these with small ritual gardens used in fertility cults of the region; others take them simply as a picture of Israel's investment in foreign alliances and ways.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1 to 6 are the oracle proper, with Damascus and Ephraim bound together and the image of a stripped harvest. Verses 7 to 11 are organized by the repeated phrase “In that day” (verses 4, 7, and 9) and contrast two ways of looking: to the Maker and the Holy One of Israel, or to altars made with human hands and fingers. Verse 10 gives the diagnosis, the heart of the chapter: “you have forgotten the God of your salvation and failed to remember the Rock of your refuge.” Verses 12 to 14 are a separate short poem full of sound (roar, rage, rumble) that builds to a sudden reversal: “In the evening, there is sudden terror”, and by morning the attackers are gone.

outline.t: Damascus a heap of ruins and Ephraim's fortress gone
The glory of Jacob fades, leaving only gleanings
People look to their Maker instead of their altars
Forsaken cities and the harvest that vanishes
The roaring nations rebuked and scattered overnight

doctrines.note: Israel trusted gods and objects it had made with its own hands. The chapter's cure is to turn one's eyes to the Maker, the one who made the people rather than the one they made.
Israel is judged alongside Damascus because it allied itself with a pagan power against God's word. Covenant privilege gives no immunity when the people forget the God of their salvation.
The nations rage like the sea, yet God rebukes them and they are driven away like chaff. The final lines assure those who are plundered that the plunderers do not have the last word.

words.note: Maoz, a stronghold, place of safety, or refuge. In verse 9 it describes Israel's strong cities, and in verse 10 it is God himself, the Rock of your refuge. The chapter plays the two against each other: the fortified cities fail because the people forgot their true stronghold.

Shaah, to look to or gaze at, with a sense of looking for help or with regard. Verses 7 and 8 use it twice: people will look to their Maker and will not look to their altars. What a person looks to in trouble shows what he trusts.

Asherah, the name of a Canaanite mother goddess and of the wooden cult objects that represented her. The Old Testament often condemns Asherah poles set up in Israel and Judah (for example 2 Kings 18:4, where Hezekiah cuts one down).

Kavod, glory, weight, honor. In verses 3 and 4 it is the splendor of the Israelites and of Jacob, which will fade and waste away. Israel's glory, taken apart from God, proves as thin as a stripped olive tree.

christ: The chapter's link to Christ is thematic. Its central call is to look away from gods made with hands to the Maker, the Holy One of Israel; the New Testament presents Jesus as the one in whom the Maker has come near and made himself known (John 1:3, 1:14). The picture of a remnant left after the harvest, a few olives at the top of the tree, fits Isaiah's steady theme that God preserves a remnant, which Paul takes up when he speaks of a remnant chosen by grace (Romans 11:5). The final poem, in which the nations rage and are scattered, is close to Psalm 2, which the early church applied to the powers that set themselves against Jesus and failed (Acts 4:25-28).

hard.q: Damascus is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. Has verse 1 been fulfilled?
hard.a: Interpreters answer in different ways. Many hold that the prophecy was fulfilled in 732 BC, when Tiglath-pileser III captured Damascus, killed its king, deported its people, and ended its independence; verse 3 speaks of sovereignty removed from Damascus, which is exactly what happened. On this view, heap of ruins is the ordinary language of conquest in ancient prophecy and inscriptions, describing a city destroyed as a kingdom's capital rather than a site never lived on again. Some readers, noting that Damascus was rebuilt and thrives, argue that verse 1 still awaits a future and final destruction, and this view is common in some popular prophecy teaching. Others see a pattern of partial fulfillment in the eighth century pointing toward God's final judgment on all powers that oppose him. The text's own horizon is the Aram and Israel of Isaiah's day, linked to the crisis of chapter 7, and that is the place to begin.

questions: Israel allied with Damascus and shared its fall. What alliances or dependencies are you tempted to trust more than God?
Verse 10 says the people forgot the God of their salvation. What habits help you remember, and what makes you forget?
The nations roar in the evening and are gone by morning. When has something that looked overwhelming turned out to be temporary?
